[RDSC.14.3.6] **`LineSpan`-emission scope.** The compiler must emit one
`LineSpan` atom per **beta** and **terminal** node it attributes to a source
construct ([RDSC.14.3.4]) — the rule-authored-construct nodes — and **none per
alpha** node. A beta node carries its introducing pattern's join tests and maps
to that pattern's source span; a terminal carries the rule's RHS and maps to
the rule's source span.

A node the compiler makes for itself carries none, and the compiler must not
invent a position for one: a capture view, a continuation's response pattern, a
timer's beta, and the terminal of an `after` follow-up or of a call's sibling
rule. Such a node is the compiler's, and a position given to it would point a
runtime diagnostic at source that does not contain the node.

An alpha node carries no `LineSpan` atom because it **belongs to no single
rule**. Its identity is `(schema_name, tests)` ([IRET.6.6]), so every
pattern in the bundle whose schema and tests coincide shares one node,
and a shared node has no single source span to name. Its source is the
schema declaration, attributed by `SchemaSource` ([RDSC.5.7]).

That reason is deliberately **independent of what an alpha carries**.
An alpha node may carry tests — [RDSC.4a.6] is the normative statement
of the test list, and a `where`-predicate over one fact and a constant
does lower onto one — so this rule must not be derived from an alpha
having no tests, nor from a rule-authored predicate never reaching one.
Sharing is the property that holds either way, so it is the one the rule
rests on.

A predicate hoisted onto a shared alpha therefore has no `LineSpan` of its
own. It is not thereby unattributable: the pattern that introduced it
is named by that pattern's own beta `LineSpan`, and the schema by `SchemaSource`. A
diagnostic naming a predicate's source reads the beta, never the alpha.

The `node_id` namespace remains `AlphaNode` / `BetaNode` / `TerminalNode`-global
([RDSC.14.3.3]); only the `LineSpan`-bearing subset is beta + terminal.
